app.name: Vacuon
app.readOnlyNotice: Vacuon deletes to the Recycle Bin by default; Shift+Del is permanent and asks for an explicit acknowledgement. The reversible quarantine of milestone M4 is still ahead, so the Recycle Bin is the only undo today.
volumes.title: VOLUMES
volumes.noMft: {0} — no MFT, scanning through the API
scan.prompt: Pick a drive and click Scan.
scan.logicalOnly: {0} logical · size on disk not measured (only the MFT exposes AllocatedSize)
scan.logicalAndDisk: {0} logical · {1} on disk · {2} of cluster slack
scan.nothingYetHint: Pick a drive above and click Scan. With administrator rights Vacuon reads the NTFS MFT straight off the volume and indexes a million files in seconds; without elevation it falls back to the Windows API, reaches the same result and takes minutes.
reconcile.agrees: agrees with the filesystem ({0}% of the used space is attributed to files)
reconcile.overcounted: BUG: {0} more than the volume reports as used. Do not trust this total.
reconcile.undercounted: only {0}% of the used space is attributed to files — the rest may be shadow copies or filesystem metadata
reconcile.undercountedWalk: only {0}% of the used space is attributed to files — a scan without Administrator cannot open every folder
reconcile.unknown: the volume reported no used space to compare against
reconcile.explainTitle: What is inflating the total (biggest claimed occupancy):
reconcile.label: Cross-check
fallback.needsElevation: reading the MFT requires running as Administrator
fallback.notNtfs: the volume is not NTFS (exFAT/FAT32/ReFS have no MFT)
fallback.mftUnreadable: the MFT could not be interpreted ({0})
elevation.notElevatedHint: Not elevated — the scan will use the Windows API (slower)
elevation.declined: Elevation declined at the UAC prompt. Vacuon keeps working, without the MFT read.
elevation.alwaysOn: Vacuon will relaunch elevated every time you open it. Windows shows the UAC prompt — there is no way to suppress it without creating a scheduled task, and that is not done behind your back.
elevation.alwaysOff: Turn on to always open elevated. Without elevation there is no MFT read, and the scan goes from seconds to minutes.
elevation.whyBody: Reading the MFT means opening the volume in raw mode (\\.\C:), and only an elevated process may do that. It is the difference between indexing a million files in seconds and taking minutes through the Windows API. Vacuon opens the volume for READING only — never for writing.

security.title: Registry persistence points
security.intro: 44 keys where malware commonly takes root: Run and RunOnce, Winlogon, AppInit_DLLs, AppCertDlls, Image File Execution Options, SilentProcessExit, LSA packages, Command Processor, Active Setup, BHOs, file associations and the Startup folder.
security.disclaimer: Read-only — no key is modified. Vacuon is not an antivirus: there is no signature database here, only behavioural heuristics with the reason always in plain sight. Legitimate entries do show up in the list; read the why before concluding anything.
security.prompt: Inspects 44 registry points where malware commonly takes root. Read-only — nothing is changed.
security.emptyHint: Click Inspect. Without administrator rights, protected HKLM keys and the Scheduled Tasks are left out — and the report says exactly that instead of passing the list off as complete.
security.notElevatedSuffix: Without elevation, protected HKLM keys and the Scheduled Tasks are left out.
settings.themeHint: The switch is immediate, no restart. Choosing “follow the system”, Vacuon reacts when you change the Windows theme with the app open.
settings.languageHint: Applies immediately. English is the default; the Portuguese translation is optional. Any string not translated yet falls back to English instead of showing a placeholder.
settings.iconSizeHint: Also switchable from the Explorer toolbar. At the larger sizes, images and videos show their real content — that is what lets you decide what to delete without opening the file.
settings.contentThumbs: Content thumbnail for images and videos
settings.contentThumbsHint: Turned off, everything uses the file type icon: instant, and it never touches the file contents.
settings.privacyNote: Not a single byte leaves this machine: there is no server, no account and no telemetry. Preferences live in {0}.
status.cannotReveal: Could not open the containing folder.
status.clipboardBusy: The clipboard is busy. Try again.
status.noSuspicious: No file matched the heuristics. That is good news.
autorun.runOnce: Runs once at the next logon and deletes itself
autorun.runOnceEx: RunOnce variant, rarely used by legitimate software
autorun.runServices: Autorun inherited from Windows 9x; modern software does not use it
autorun.runServicesOnce: Autorun inherited from Windows 9x, single execution
autorun.policiesRun: Autorun through group policy — outside a domain, that is a red flag
autorun.winlogonShell: The Windows shell. Anything other than explorer.exe is a hijack
autorun.winlogonUserinit: User initialization process. Extra commands here run at every logon
autorun.winlogonTaskman: Alternative task manager. Normally does not exist
autorun.appInitDlls: DLLs loaded into EVERY process that uses user32.dll. Should be empty
autorun.appInitDlls32: AppInit_DLLs in the 32-bit view. Should be empty
autorun.appCertDlls: DLLs loaded on every process creation. Normally does not exist
autorun.bootExecute: Run by the session manager before logon
autorun.ifeoDebugger: Debugger attached to an executable: running program X runs program Y
autorun.silentProcessExit: Process triggered when another one exits — a persistence technique
autorun.lsaPackage: {0}: DLLs loaded by LSASS. A classic credential-theft target
autorun.fileAssociation: Open command for {0}. Altered, it runs malware alongside any file of that type
autorun.commandProcessor: Command run on every cmd.exe launch
autorun.commandProcessorUser: Command run on every cmd.exe launch (current user)
autorun.bho: Browser Helper Objects (Internet Explorer). A historic adware vector
autorun.shellServiceObject: COM objects loaded by Explorer at startup
autorun.activeSetup: Active Setup: runs once per user at first logon
autorun.startupFolder: Startup folder. Redirecting this hides the user's autoruns
autorun.logonScript: Script run at user logon. Not created by ordinary software
autorun.accessDeniedReason: Key could not be read without Administrator rights — run elevated to inspect it
autorun.orphan: The file it points to does not exist — orphaned autorun
autorun.unsigned: Binary without a valid digital signature
heuristic.hiddenWindow: PowerShell started with a hidden window
heuristic.downloadAndRun: Downloads and runs content from the internet
heuristic.urlInCommand: URL embedded in the autorun command line
heuristic.lolbinOutside: Uses {0} as an intermediary outside the system directory
heuristic.certutil: certutil used to decode or download a file
heuristic.volatileFolder: Executable sits in a volatile folder ({0})
heuristic.scriptInProfile: Autorun points to a script (vbs/js/ps1/bat) in the user profile
file.rlo: Name contains a Unicode text-reversal character (RLO) — a classic trick to hide the real extension
file.doubleExtension: Double extension: looks like a {0} file but is executable ({1})
file.spacePadding: Long run of spaces in the name, hiding the executable extension
file.executableWithAds: Executable with a {0} KB Alternate Data Stream — content invisible in Explorer
file.phishingExtension: The {0} extension is rare in legitimate software and common in malicious attachments
file.recentSystem32: executable created in System32 within the last 30 days

delete.blockedHeader: {0} items are protected and will be skipped

delete.allBlocked: Every selected item is protected. Nothing was deleted.
delete.recycledOne: 1 item moved to the Recycle Bin · {0} stays occupied until you empty it
delete.recycled: {0} items moved to the Recycle Bin · {1} stays occupied until you empty it

filter.includeFoldersHint: Folders are matched by name and sized by everything inside them. Turned off by an extension filter, since a folder has no extension.
security.experimentalBody: This module is the newest part of Vacuon and the least settled. It has no signature database — only behavioural rules — and on an elevated full-volume scan it reaches files a normal scan never sees, so the count can be high. Treat every finding as “worth a look”, never as a verdict, and do not delete anything on its word alone.
security.falsePositiveNote: A false positive here is treated as a bug. If something legitimate shows up, please report it.

snapshot.usedNoChanges: nothing changed since the snapshot, taken {0} ago
snapshot.saved: snapshot saved — the next open starts from a journal delta
snapshot.refusedNoSnapshot: no snapshot for this volume yet
snapshot.refusedUnusable: the snapshot is from another format version

memory.title: What is using this machine's memory
memory.intro: Measured now, grouped by program and ranked by private memory — the figure that answers who is actually holding the RAM.
memory.honestyNote: Working set is what Task Manager shows, and it counts pages shared between processes once for each of them, so adding it up across a browser's children gives a total larger than the machine has. Private memory is the one that adds up.
memory.prompt: Click Inspect to measure. Nothing is changed until you ask.
memory.compressedNote: Pages Windows compressed and kept in memory instead of writing them to disk. It looks like waste in a process list and is the opposite — it is the reason those pages did not become disk reads.
memory.load: {0}% in use, as Windows reports it
memory.fromStartupTotal: {0} of what is in use belongs to programs Windows launches at sign-in. Turning one off in Startup removes it for good; nothing on this screen can.
memory.trimExplain: This is the button other utilities call "free memory". It empties working sets, and the available figure goes up — but nothing was freed. The pages moved to the standby list or the pagefile and come back, from disk, the moment their program touches them again. On a machine that is not short of memory it usually makes things slower, not faster.
memory.trimResult: {0} processes trimmed · available moved by {1}. Those pages went to disk or standby, and return when their programs need them.
memory.trimResultNegative: {0} processes trimmed · available actually went DOWN by {1}. Windows pulled pages back in. This is what the number looks like when nobody rounds it in their favour.
memory.closeProtected: Windows needs this one; Vacuon will not close it
memory.closed: Closed. It was holding {0}, and available memory rose by {1}.
memory.closedPartial: {0} of {1} processes closed. They were holding {2}, and available memory rose by {3}.
memory.closeDenied: Access denied — that process runs at a higher level than Vacuon. Restart elevated and try again.
memory.closeStillRunning: The close was issued and the process is still there. Nothing is being claimed.

ai.title: Microsoft AI components
ai.intro: Windows ships a number of AI features, and turns several of them on without asking. This tab reads the state of each one and can switch off the ones Microsoft documents a control for.
ai.disclaimer: Only Microsoft components appear here. Third-party AI software on this machine is none of this tab's business, however much of it there is.
ai.honestyNote: Vacuon writes the documented value and reads it back to confirm it is there. Whether Windows acts on it right away or only after you sign out is up to Windows, and this tab will not claim otherwise.
ai.journalNote: Every change is written to {0} before the registry is touched, so Undo always has something to restore.
ai.prompt: Click Inspect to read the current state. Nothing is changed until you ask.
ai.summary: {0} components · {1} still on · {2} measured in memory right now
ai.summaryNothingRunning: {0} components · {1} still on · none of them is running right now
ai.reportedOnly: Reported only — removing a shipped package is a servicing operation, not a checkbox.
ai.returnsAfterUpdate: Windows Update is known to put this one back.
ai.outcomeApplied: Turned off, and the value was read back to confirm it.
ai.outcomeUndone: Put back the way it was found.
ai.outcomeNoChange: Already in that state; nothing was written.
ai.outcomeNeedsElevation: This one lives under HKLM and needs Administrator. Restart elevated and try again.
ai.outcomeNotConfirmed: The write went through but reading it back did not return it. Nothing is being claimed.

startup.title: Programs Windows launches at sign-in
startup.intro: Everything Windows starts for you, from the Run keys and the Startup folders, with what each one is holding in memory right now.
startup.honestyNote: Turning one off writes the same switch Task Manager and Settings use, so the entry stays where its program put it and Windows is simply told to skip it. Nothing is deleted, and turning it back on is one click.

startup.outcomeDisabled: Disabled. Windows will skip it at the next sign-in.
startup.outcomeNeedsElevation: This one is machine-wide and needs Administrator. Restart elevated and try again.
startup.outcomeNotConfirmed: The write went through but reading it back did not return it. Nothing is being claimed.
